source_text: Nec diutius de isto, si idem est Paulus qui et alibi haereses inter carnalia crimina numerat scribens ad Galatas, et qui Tito suggerit hominem haereticum post primam correptionem recusandum, quod perversus sit eiusmodi et delinquat, ut a semetipso damnatus. Sed et in omni paene epistula de adulterinis doctrinis fugiendis inculcans haereses taxat. Quarum opera sunt adulterae doctrinae, haereses dictae Graeca voce, ex interpretatione electionis qua quis sive ad instituendas sive ad suscipiendas eas utitur. Ideo et sibi damnatum dixit haereticum, quia et in quo damnatur sibi elegit. Nobis vere nihil ex nostro arbitrio indulgere licet, sed nec eligere quod aliquis de arbitrio suo induxerit. Apostolos domini habemus auctores, qui nec ipsi quicquam ex suo arbitrio quod inducerent elegerunt, sed acceptam a Christo disciplinam fideliter nationibus assignaverunt. Itaque etiam si angelus de caelis aliter evangelizaret, anathema diceretur a nobis. Providerat iam tunc spiritus sanctus futurum in virgin(??) quadam Philumene angelum seductionis, transfigurantem se in angelum lucis, cuius signis et praestigiis Apelles inductus novam haeresin induxit.
thought_title: Paul condemns heretics and the Spirit foretold Apelles
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that heresies were already condemned by the apostles, and he now cites Paul's letters and the case of Apelles as proof.
pass_a_gloss: Not longer about this, if the same is Paul who also elsewhere numbers heresies among fleshly crimes writing to the Galatians, and who suggests to Titus that a heretical man after a first correction is to be refused, because perverse is of such a kind and sins, as one condemned by himself. But also in almost every letter, inculcating that adulterous doctrines are to be fled, he censures heresies. Of which the works are adulterous doctrines, heresies called by a Greek word, from the interpretation of choice by which someone uses them either for establishing or for taking them up. Therefore also he said a heretic condemned by himself, because also in that in which he is condemned he chose for himself. For us truly nothing from our own judgment is allowed to indulge, but not even to choose what someone from his own judgment has introduced. We have the apostles of the Lord as authors, who neither themselves chose anything from their own judgment which they would introduce, but the discipline received from Christ they faithfully assigned to the nations. Therefore even if an angel from the heavens should evangelize otherwise, anathema would be said by us. The Holy Spirit had already foreseen then that there would be in a certain virgin Philumene an angel of seduction, transforming himself into an angel of light, by whose signs and tricks Apelles was induced and introduced a new heresy.

pass_b_english: There is no need to dwell on this further. The same Paul numbers heresies among fleshly crimes when he writes to the Galatians (Galatians 5:19-21), and he advises Titus that a heretical man is to be refused after a first correction, because such a person is perverse and sins, being condemned by himself (Titus 3:10-11). In almost every letter, moreover, he insists that adulterous doctrines are to be fled, and in doing so he censures heresies. The works of heresies are adulterous doctrines. The Greek word "heresies" comes from the meaning of choice, which a person uses either to establish such doctrines or to adopt them. That is why he said the heretic is condemned by himself: because he has chosen for himself the very thing in which he is condemned.

For us, however, nothing from our own judgment is allowed to indulge, nor may we choose what someone has introduced from his own judgment. We have the Lord's apostles as our authors, and they themselves did not choose anything from their own judgment to introduce, but faithfully assigned to the nations the discipline they had received from Christ. Therefore, even if an angel from heaven should evangelize differently, he would be declared anathema by us (Galatians 1:8).

The Holy Spirit had already foreseen that in a certain virgin named Philumene there would come an angel of seduction, transforming himself into an angel of light. Apelles, induced by his signs and tricks, introduced a new heresy.
notes: The source text has '(??)' after 'virgin' indicating uncertainty in the manuscript; the gloss renders it as 'a certain virgin Philumene' following the brief's description of Philumene as a virgin (text uncertain).

last_rejected.quote: The works of heresies are adulterous doctrines; the Greek word "heresies" comes from the meaning of choice, which a person uses either to establish such doctrines or to adopt them.
last_rejected.source_quote: Quarum opera sunt adulterae doctrinae, haereses dictae Graeca voce, ex interpretatione electionis qua quis sive ad instituendas sive ad suscipiendas eas utitur.
last_rejected.why: Source says heresies are named in Greek from the meaning of 'choice' by which one uses [choice] either to establish or adopt them; English says person uses 'choice' to establish 'doctrines', losing the reflexive structure.
last_rejected.fix: The works of heresies are adulterous doctrines; 'heresies,' named in Greek from the meaning of 'choice,' is what one uses either to establish or to adopt them.
last_rejected.ruling: English shifts 'establish' from heresies to doctrines but overall meaning (choice used to create or adopt heresies) remains.

last_rejected.quote: because he has chosen for himself the very thing in which he is condemned
last_rejected.source_quote: quia et in quo damnatur sibi elegit
last_rejected.why: Source says 'he has chosen for himself that by which he is condemned'; English 'the very thing in which' is awkward and slightly shifts sense from means to container.
last_rejected.fix: because he has chosen for himself the very thing by which he is condemned
last_rejected.ruling: Translation matches Latin 'in quo damnatur sibi elegit' – 'chosen for himself the thing in which he is condemned.'

last_rejected.quote: nothing from our own judgment is allowed to indulge
last_rejected.source_quote: Nobis vere nihil ex nostro arbitrio indulgere licet
last_rejected.why: Ungrammatical English: 'nothing...is allowed to indulge' lacks a subject for 'indulge'; source means 'we are not permitted to indulge anything from our own judgment.'
last_rejected.fix: we are by no means permitted to indulge anything from our own judgment
last_rejected.ruling: Awkward phrasing but conveys same meaning: we may not indulge anything from our own judgment.

last_rejected.why: Tertullian does not cite Galatians 5:19‑21; those verses list works of the flesh, not heresies.
last_rejected.ruling: Galatians 5:20 lists haereses among carnalia crimina; translator's Scripture reference is accurate, not wrong.

polish.changed: Clarified the flow by separating the argument into three paragraphs, made the subject of each sentence explicit, and smoothed the transition to the Philumene passage so her role as the vehicle of the seducing angel is clear.
